cells.tense: You are moving toward what pulls you right now, with the pen already in your hand.
cells.act: follow a raw curiosity with no use for it
cells.ask: Chase down whatever flickers your interest this week — no purpose attached, an hour of it, no checking where it goes.
cells.core:
Under the pull toward what you want, you listen to it before you try to name it. That is rare, and it is working. The next steps keep arriving because they ride the same current, and the direction holds because you do not stop to argue with your own interest. When something catches you, following it turns out to open the next useful door — the pattern keeps holding.

This week, chase down one spark of plain interest and give it an hour, no practical use, no question of where it is going. You do not locate the pull by pointing at it; you locate it by walking one step in a direction that feels alive, then looking at what you are standing in. Either it lands in something real or it does not, and either way you will have sharpened what you are listening for.

cells.tense: You're already charging at something that hasn't happened yet, bracing for a race you haven't entered.
cells.act: think it through to its sharp point
cells.ask: Before you move on whatever you're running at hardest, write the reasoning down to its plainest edge on a page, then decide.
cells.core:
When the light pulls you, you often move before the light has settled. That energy is real and it carried you before. Right now it runs past the thing it is meant to serve: the plan gets brighter, the starting line keeps moving back, and the doing gets thinner. Bracing has replaced direction. The urge to charge is still there, but it is no longer sure what it is charging.

Before the next move on the big thing pulling you, stop and sharpen the thinking to its point. Reduce it to one page — the logic, the tradeoff, the actual choice. If the page holds, go. If it does not hold, that plain page has just saved you a week of pushing. The charge does its best work when it knows where it is landing.

cells.tense: You stood at the starting line and you're still standing there, with the race already behind you.
cells.act: move the structure one real inch
cells.ask: Toward what's pulling you, send the email, open the first page, or make the first call — only that step, part of the plan or not.
cells.core:
The pull you were following has gone quiet. You still want the thing — that is clear — but it does not reach your hands anymore, and the starting line sits behind you. Maybe you moved toward it once and stopped when the next thing arrived. Maybe you are waiting for the light to feel as bright as it did. Either way nothing is being carried, and the pull shows up only when you glance at it.

Start with one real inch. Not the whole plan, not the version you would be proud of, just one action small enough to do without extra energy: one page, one email, one call. Do it once. That single inch tells you whether the thing is still alive. If it is, the next inch comes easier. If it is not, you will know, without handing it another year of standing.

cells.tense: You're setting direction in a room you're already leading, and the pen is down where you left it.
cells.act: release what is done and keep what serves
cells.ask: Go through the projects and roles you still call yours this week; let the finished ones go, keep the rest.
cells.core:
You are drawn toward something bright, and that pull shapes how you choose what to keep. You also have a way of not naming what holding it has cost. Projects that no longer serve sit in the load, and the way you describe them is that they are still useful — until they are not, and time goes by before anyone says so plainly. The direction is real. The load is heavier than the direction needs.

Look at what you are holding and ask one question of each: is it done or is it serving? Let the finished ones go. Keep the ones that still work, and say to yourself, once, plainly, why you are keeping them. Clearing is the move this week. Not the push, not a new direction. Clearing, so the next charge has somewhere to land.
cells.sheetLine: The pull is real. So is the weight you've stopped naming.
